days.title: Functions, Slopes & One-Dimensional Kinematics (Position vs. Time)
days.overview: Slope of a function measures how fast output changes — the same idea as velocity, which is how fast position changes with time.

math.lesson: A function f(x) assigns exactly one output to each input. The slope between two points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) is m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). For a line y = mx + b, m is constant. Average rate of change over [a, b] is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).

example.prompt: Find the slope of y = 3x − 5 between x = 1 and x = 4.

videos.title: Derivative as Slope of a Tangent Line

problems.prompt: What is the slope of f(x) = 2x + 7 between x = 0 and x = 5?
problems.hint: For a line, slope equals the coefficient of x.
problems.solution: The slope is 2, matching the coefficient in y = 2x + 7.

hints.concept: For a line, slope equals the coefficient of x.
hints.setup: Start: Identify two points: (0, 7) and (5, 17). Substitute into m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

problems.prompt: A car's position is x(t) = 4t + 10 (meters). What is its average velocity from t = 0 to t = 6 s?
problems.hint: Average velocity equals the slope of x vs. t.

hints.concept: Average velocity equals the slope of x vs. t.
hints.setup: Start: x(0) = 10, x(6) = 34. Substitute into v_avg = Δx / Δt.

physics.lesson: One-dimensional kinematics describes motion along a straight line. Position x(t) tells where an object is. Displacement Δx = x_f − x_i. Average velocity v_avg = Δx/Δt. For constant velocity, x(t) = x₀ + vt — a linear function of time.

steps: Define velocity: v = Δx/Δt for constant v

days.title: Introduction to Limits & Instantaneous Velocity
days.overview: Limits describe what a function approaches — the calculus foundation for instantaneous velocity at a single moment.

math.lesson: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is the value f(x) gets close to (not necessarily f(a)). Notation: lim(x→a) f(x) = L. Limits let us define the derivative as a limit of difference quotients.

videos.title: Limits, L'Hôpital's Rule, and Epsilon-Delta Definitions

problems.prompt: What is lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3)?

hints.setup: Start: (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x+3. Substitute into (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x+3.

problems.prompt: Evaluate lim(x→0) (5x)/x.

hints.setup: Start: 5x/x = 5. Substitute into 5x/x = 5.

physics.lesson: Average velocity v_avg = Δx/Δt uses a time interval. Instantaneous velocity at time t is the limit as Δt → 0: v(t) = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt. This is the slope of the tangent to the x vs. t curve.

derivation.title: Instantaneous Velocity from a Limit
steps: Instantaneous velocity: v(t) = lim(Δt→0) [x(t + Δt) − x(t)]/Δt
This limit is the derivative dx/dt
Graphically: tangent slope to x(t) at time t

days.title: The Power Rule for Derivatives & Acceleration Equations
days.overview: The power rule turns position functions into velocity and acceleration — linking derivatives directly to kinematics.

math.lesson: If f(x) = xⁿ, then f′(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹ (power rule). Constant rule: d/dx(c) = 0. Sum rule: derivative of a sum is sum of derivatives. These rules let us differentiate polynomials quickly.

steps: Apply power rule term by term

physics.lesson: With x(t) known, v(t) = dx/dt and a(t) = dv/dt = d²x/dt². For constant acceleration a, integrating twice gives v(t) = v₀ + at and x(t) = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² — the AP kinematics equations.

days.title: Derivative Rules (Product & Quotient) & Advanced Motion Graphs
days.overview: Product and quotient rules handle complex rates of change, while motion graphs connect derivatives to physical meaning.

math.lesson: Product rule: (fg)′ = f′g + fg′. Quotient rule: (f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g². Use these when functions are multiplied or divided rather than added.

days.title: The Chain Rule & 2D Kinematics (Projectile Motion)
days.overview: The chain rule differentiates composed functions — essential for projectile motion where horizontal and vertical components depend on time.

math.lesson: Chain rule: if y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). In Leibniz form: dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx). Used whenever one function is inside another.

videos.title: Visualizing the Chain Rule and Product Rule

hints.setup: Start: f′=2u·2x=4x(x²+1). Substitute into f′=2u·2x=4x(x²+1).

physics.lesson: Projectile motion treats horizontal and vertical motion independently. x(t) = v₀ cosθ · t, y(t) = v₀ sinθ · t − ½gt². Acceleration is constant: a_x = 0, a_y = −g. Range R = v₀² sin(2θ)/g.

days.title: Trig Functions & Vector Components in Physics
days.overview: Trigonometry gives the language for angles and components — vectors in physics are built from sine and cosine.

days.title: Vector Dot Products & Work Done by a Constant Force
days.overview: The dot product measures alignment of vectors — work is force times displacement in the direction of motion.

math.lesson: Dot product: a · b = |a||b| cos θ = a_x b_x + a_y b_y. Result is a scalar. Orthogonal vectors have dot product 0. Projection of a onto b: comp_b(a) = (a·b)/|b|.

Start: 5·4·0.5=10. Substitute into 5·4·0.5=10.

physics.lesson: Work by constant force: W = F · d = Fd cos θ, where θ is the angle between F and displacement. Only the parallel component does work. SI unit: joule (J = N·m).

derivation.title: Work as a Dot Product
steps: Decompose F into parallel and perpendicular to d
Only F_parallel = F cos θ does work
W = F_parallel · d = Fd cos θ
In vector form: W = F · d

days.title: Introduction to Anti-Derivatives (Indefinite Integrals) & Finding Position from Acceleration

math.lesson: Indefinite integral ∫f(x)dx = F(x) + C where F′(x)=f(x). Power rule reverse: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C (n≠−1). Always include +C for indefinite integrals.
